newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French PIBOR three-month interest rate contracts settled higher with the franc on Wednesday but bond futures dipped into the red following U.S. Chicago NAPM data after hitting a contract high earlier in the day

U.S. influence will be absent on Thursday, with the market closed for the Thanksgiving holiday but traders said the French market was still strong, helped by a receding threat of labour conflict spreading as protesting truckers looked nearer a deal.
The December bond future settled down 0.02 at 128.08 after a contract high of 128.28 earlier, sliding into the red after the U.S. data on profit-taking and U.S. pre-holiday selling.

Talks in the truck drivers dispute resumed at 1545 GMT, on the tenth day of their blockade protest, after trade union and government officials said there was substantial progress on two of the truckers main demands, retirement at 55 instead of 60 and shorter work hours.
The truckers also want higher pay.

The Chicagoland Business Barometer increased to a seasonally adjusted 57.6 in November -- above 50 suggests that the economy is expanding -- from 56.9 in October. This came at the same time as stronger-then-expected U.S. October durable goods orders data, showing a rise of 0.1 percent.

French preliminary GDP figures for the third quarter are due out at 0745 GMT and are expected to show robust growth, boosted by car-buying ahead of the September 30 expiry of the Jupette sales incentive scheme.
A Reuter poll of 10 economists on Wednesday gave a consensus forecast of a 0.9 percent rise on the second quarter and a range of 0.7-1.3 percent. Second quarter growth fell 0.4 percent.

The Bank of France's monetary policy council meets in the morning but the widespread view is that it will leave interest rates as they are, even if traders said some were not absolutely ruling out the possibility of a minor easing gesture.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe weighed into the currency policy debate, started by ex President Valery Giscard d'Estaing last week, to say franc-mark parity should not be changed.

"Should the franc-mark parity be changed? I don't think so. Any devaluation is a national improverishment," he said in the National Assembly. He repeated that "the dollar is evidently undervalued" and gave U.S. companies an unfair advantage.
Giscard d'Estaing said France and Germany could follow different monetary policies. "They must not be subordinated, that is to say, one does not necessarily have to follow the other," he said.
